The year 2023 was nothing short of historic for Shah Rukh Khan. After a four-year hiatus from leading roles, the superstar returned with Pathaan, which collected Rs. 1,050.30 crores worldwide, followed by Jawan, which went a step further with a staggering Rs. 1,148.32 crores. Together, the two films amassed nearly Rs. 2,200 crores globally, reaffirming his position as one of Indian cinema's biggest superstars. Three years later, Shah Rukh Khan is gearing up for his next theatrical release, King, directed by Siddharth Anand and scheduled to hit cinemas on December 24, 2026.
The biggest competitor for King is not another superstar or another film. It is Shah Rukh Khan’s own box-office history
The excitement surrounding King is understandable. The film reunites Shah Rukh Khan with his Pathaan director, promises high-octane action and features an ensemble cast including Deepika Padukone, Suhana Khan and Abhishek Bachchan. However, beneath all the anticipation lies an interesting question: Has Shah Rukh Khan raised the bar so extraordinarily high that even a hugely successful film might now be considered a disappointment?
Before Pathaan and Jawan, a worldwide collection of Rs. 300-400 crores was considered an impressive achievement for many Bollywood films. But Shah Rukh Khan changed the conversation by delivering two consecutive Rs. 1,000 crore blockbusters, and in doing so, possibly created an unusually high benchmark for himself.
Today, the discussion around King isn't merely about whether it will succeed. Fans and trade observers are already speculating about whether it can cross Rs. 1,000 crores, surpass Pathaan or even challenge Jawan. Imagine a scenario where King collects Rs. 600-700 crores worldwide. Such numbers would be extraordinary for most Hindi films, yet there is a possibility that sections of the industry and social media would term the performance underwhelming simply because Shah Rukh Khan has delivered bigger hits in the past.
Ironically, King may find its biggest competition not in another film or superstar, but in Shah Rukh Khan's own box-office records.
Adding to the expectations is the film's reported scale. In July, Bollywood Hungama reported that King was being mounted on a production budget of approximately Rs. 450 crores, excluding publicity expenses and Shah Rukh Khan's remuneration. Siddharth Anand subsequently disputed the circulating budget reports, and hence, the actual cost remains unconfirmed. Nevertheless, the film is being positioned as an ambitious action spectacle, and its commercial performance will naturally attract considerable attention.

The Christmas and New Year holidays provide an excellent opportunity for a huge opening, but December 2026 is packed with major releases, including Hollywood spectacles like Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three. Bimbisāra (in Buddhist tradition) or Shrenika (Śreṇika) and Seniya (Seṇiya) in the Jain histories[2][3] (c. 558 – c. 491 BCE[4][5] or c. 472 – c. 405 BCE[6][7]) was the King of Magadha (r. 543 – 492 BCE[8] or r. 457 – 405 BCE[6][9]) and belonged to the Haryanka dynasty.[10] He was the son of Bhattiya.[11] His expansion of the kingdom, especially his annexation of the kingdom of Anga to the east, is considered to have laid the foundations for the later expansion of the Mauryan Empire.[12]
According to Jain tradition, he is said to be the first tirthankara (Padmanabha/Mahapadma) out of the 24 tirthankaras of the future cosmic age.[13] He frequently visited the Samavasarana of Mahavira seeking answers to his queries.[14]
According to Buddhist Tradition, he is also known for his cultural achievements and was a great friend and protector of the Buddha. According to the 7th-century Chinese monk Xuanzang, Bimbisara built the city of Rajgir (Rajagriha).[8] He was succeeded on the throne by his son Ajatashatru.[12]
Bimbisara was the son of Bhattiya, a chieftain. He ascended to throne at the age of 15 in 543 BCE.[15] He established the Haryanka dynasty and laid the foundations of Magadha with the fortification of a village, which later became the city of Pataliputra.[16] Bimbisara's first capital was at Girivraja (identified with Rajagriha). He led a military campaign against Anga, perhaps to avenge his father's earlier defeat at the hands of its king, Brahmadatta. The campaign was successful, Anga was annexed, and prince Kunika (Ajatashatru) was appointed governor at Champa.[17] His conquest of Anga gave Magadha control over the routes to the Ganges Delta, which had important ports that gave access to the eastern coast of India.[18][19] Pukkusati, the king of Gandhara, sent Bimbisara an embassy.[15]
His court is said to have included Sona Kolivisa, Sumana (flower gatherer), Koliya (minister), Kumbhaghosaka (treasurer) and Jivaka (physician).[20]
Bimbisara used marriage alliances to strengthen his position. His first wife was Kosala Devi, the daughter of Mahā Kosala, the king of Kosala, and a sister of Prasenajit.[21] His bride brought him Kashi as dowry.[22] This marriage also ended the hostility between Magadha and Kosala and gave him a free hand in dealing with the other states. His second wife, Chellana, was a Licchavi princess from Vaishali and daughter of the Jain[23] king Chetaka.[24] His third wife, Kshema, was a daughter of the chief of the Madra clan of Punjab.[25] Mahavagga depicts him having 500 wives.[15]
As per Buddhism, due to influence by Devadatta (a separatist Buddhist monk), Bimbisāra was assassinated by his son Ajatashatru in c. 493 BCE, who then succeeded him to the throne. However, as per Jainism, Bimbisāra committed suicide.[18]

Where is king shrenik now
According to Jain tradition, King Shrenik (also known as Bimbisara) was a devoted follower of Lord Mahavira. Jain scriptures narrate that King Shrenik, due to some remnants of his karmas, could not attain liberation (moksha) in his lifetime despite his devotion and meritorious deeds.
As per Jain texts, particularly the Uttaradhyayana Sutra and commentaries by Jain Acharyas, it is believed that King Shrenik was reborn as a celestial being (deva) in the Sarvarthasiddhi Vimana, a heavenly abode in the upper world. It is also mentioned that in the future, after exhausting his lifespan in heaven, King Shrenik will be reborn as a human and will attain liberation (moksha) as a Kevali named King Megha in the next era.
Thus, in the context of Jain belief, King Shrenik is currently in the Sarvarthasiddhi Vimana, awaiting his future rebirth and ultimate liberation.

Quick Answer
Shrenik was a king during the time of Lord Mahavira who sought to destroy his bad karmas and avoid hell in his next life. He approached a Jain layman, Punia Shravak, to obtain the punya (merit) of his spiritual practice, Samayika.
Detailed Answer
King Shrenik is a historical figure mentioned in Jain literature as a ruler who was deeply concerned about the consequences of his karmas and the fate of his soul after death. According to the Jain story, he was willing to give up his entire kingdom to acquire the punya karma of a Jain layperson, Punia Shravak, particularly the merit earned through the practice of Samayika, a form of meditation and spiritual discipline. However, Punia Shravak explained to King Shrenik that good karma cannot be transferred or purchased; it must be earned personally through one's own righteous actions and spiritual practices. This story highlights the Jain principle that spiritual merit is individually earned and cannot be bought or transferred.
